subject: spanish
title: The café with the impossible queue
setup: You have two minutes before your train. The café worker is kind, fast, and speaking entirely in Spanish. Can you leave with the right coffee?
win: You leave with a coffee and a new trick: when you're lost, repair the conversation instead of guessing.
detour: You made it through the café. Next time, asking one clear question will save more time than an elaborate guess.

beats.scene: The worker says something too quickly. You catch exactly zero words. The queue is moving.
beats.question: What do you say?

options.label: ¿Puede repetirlo más despacio, por favor?
options.after: She slows down immediately. No one in the queue even blinks.
options.why: You asked her to repeat more slowly, politely and specifically. That's better than pretending you understood.

options.label: Sí, gracias.
options.after: She smiles, but she still doesn't know what you want.
options.why: Sí means yes. It can't repair a question you never understood, and you may be agreeing to something unexpected.

options.label: Un café, por favor.
options.after: A coffee is now on the order, but her original question is still unanswered.
options.why: A new order doesn't tell the worker which detail you missed. A repeat request keeps the conversation on track.

beats.scene: She repeats: «¿Para aquí o para llevar?» The train is close enough to hear.
beats.question: You want the coffee to go. Your reply?

options.label: Para llevar, por favor.
options.after: She reaches for a takeaway cup. Exactly right.
options.why: Para llevar means to go. Para aquí means to have it here.

options.label: Para aquí, por favor.
options.after: She puts a ceramic cup on the counter. The train is not waiting.
options.why: Para aquí means for here. It's a perfectly natural phrase—just not the choice you wanted.

options.label: Sí.
options.after: She asks the question again. There were two options to choose between.
options.why: You can't resolve an either/or question with a bare yes.

beats.scene: Holding the cup, she checks: «¿Para llevar?» This time it's a yes-or-no confirmation.
beats.question: What finishes the exchange?

options.label: Sí, para llevar.
options.after: Cup, lid, train. You made it.
options.why: Now sí is useful: you're confirming a specific suggestion. The accent distinguishes yes from si ('if').

options.label: ¿Para aquí o para llevar?
options.after: You repeat her question back. She gives you a puzzled look.
options.why: Repeating the two options isn't an answer. Now she needs confirmation.

options.label: Si para llevar.
options.after: She understands your meaning, but your written note is missing something.
options.why: For an affirmative yes, Spanish spells it sí with an accent. The unaccented si means if.

subject: piano
title: You're in the band now
setup: The drummer counts you in at 60 beats per minute. You have eight beats to sound like you've rehearsed—even though you just sat down.
win: The groove held together. The trick wasn't playing more notes; it was giving every sound and silence its time.
detour: The band kept playing, and you heard where the timing drifted. A rest is part of the music—not a blank to rush past.

beats.scene: Bar one: play C on beat 1, rest on beat 2, then play D on beat 3. The drummer starts.
beats.question: On beat 2, you should…

options.label: Stay silent for the full beat.
options.after: The drummer nods. The gap gives the D room to land.
options.why: A rest occupies time even when no key sounds. Count beat 2 silently.

options.label: Keep C sounding because you played it on beat 1.
options.after: The gap disappears, and the phrase feels crowded.
options.why: If the score calls for a rest, the earlier key must be released. A rest isn't a held note.

options.label: Skip straight to D.
options.after: D arrives early. The drummer's pulse is still on beat 2.
options.why: Skipping a silent beat shortens the bar; silence has a measured duration.

beats.scene: The tempo is 60 BPM. C starts at 0 seconds. D belongs on beat 3.
beats.question: When should D begin?

options.label: At 2.0 seconds.
options.after: D lands with the click. You and the drummer sound like a unit.
options.why: At 60 BPM each beat takes one second: beat 1 at 0, beat 2 at 1, beat 3 at 2.

options.label: At 3.0 seconds.
options.after: D lands after the intended beat. The drummer has moved on.
options.why: We count beat 1 at time zero, not at the end of the first second.

options.label: At 1.0 second.
options.after: D turns the rest into a blink.
options.why: One second after C is the start of beat 2, which must be silent.

beats.scene: Bar two puts D on the spoken 'and' between beats 1 and 2. The drummer says 'one-and-two-and'.
beats.question: At 60 BPM, how long after C does D arrive?

options.label: Half a second.
options.after: You land on the offbeat. The rhythm suddenly swings into place.
options.why: An 'and' subdivision splits a one-second beat into halves. D comes at 0.5 seconds.

options.label: One second.
options.after: D lands on beat 2, not on the 'and'.
options.why: A full second is one whole beat at this tempo. The 'and' falls halfway through.

options.label: Two seconds.
options.after: The melody is already at the next phrase when D arrives.
options.why: Two seconds is two complete beats, too late for the first 'and'.

subject: chess
title: The king's dramatic exit
setup: Your king is tired of the center. A rook is waiting in the corner. You have one chance to castle safely, but Black has plans.
win: The king reaches safety because you checked the whole route, not just the destination.
detour: Your king survives the lesson. The memorable rule: castling is about where the king travels, not only where it lands.

beats.scene: White is ready to castle kingside. The rook is on h1 and the king is on e1.
beats.question: Where does the king land after O-O?

options.label: g1
options.after: The king slides two squares to g1. A proper royal escape.
options.why: Kingside castling moves the white king e1 → g1. It is a special two-square king move.

options.label: f1
options.after: The king stops one square short and wonders where the rook went.
options.why: f1 is the rook's destination in kingside castling, not the king's.

options.label: h1
options.after: The king has wandered into the rook's starting square.
options.why: h1 is where the rook starts. The king must end on g1.

beats.scene: The king has reached g1. The rook still needs its part of the move.
beats.question: Where does the rook finish?

options.label: f1
options.after: Rook to f1. The two pieces form a compact shelter.
options.why: On white kingside castling, the rook goes h1 → f1, passing across the king's old route.

options.label: e1
options.after: The rook parks in the king's old square. That's not how castling works.
options.why: The rook stops on f1, immediately on the other side of the king.

options.label: g1
options.after: The king has already taken that square; the pieces would collide.
options.why: King g1 and rook f1 are the final arrangement.

beats.scene: Rewind. Black puts a rook on f8, with the entire f-file open. White's king is not in check on e1.
beats.question: Can White castle through f1?

options.label: No. f1 is attacked.
options.after: You stop the castle. The king avoids walking through the rook's line of fire.
options.why: The king may not castle out of, through, or into check. An attacked crossing square f1 makes this illegal.

options.label: Yes. g1 itself is safe.
options.after: The arbiter stops your hand mid-castle.
options.why: Checking only the destination misses the king's path. The attacked crossing square f1 matters.

options.label: Yes, if the rook moves first.
options.after: The arbiter says that's two separate moves, not a castle.
options.why: Castling is one special king-and-rook move. You can't rearrange the order to escape the attacked-square rule.

subject: calculus
title: The festival banner is growing
setup: You're designing an enormous festival banner. Two edges are stretching at once, and the printer wants to know how quickly the area is growing.
win: You saved the print order. Both expanding edges contribute strips of new area—and they add.
detour: You caught the surprise: when two sizes change together, the new area comes from two strips, not a product of two speeds.

beats.scene: Right now the banner is 3 metres long and 4 metres wide. Its length grows at 1 m/s; its width grows at 4 m/s.
beats.question: How much new area per second comes from the changing length alone?

options.label: 4 m²/s
options.after: A long, skinny strip appears at the right edge of the banner.
options.why: Length grows by 1 metre per second across the current width of 4 metres: 1 × 4 = 4 m²/s.

options.label: 1 m²/s
options.after: The printer points out that a strip has a width as well as a growth rate.
options.why: A length rate by itself is m/s. Multiply it by the other edge's current size to obtain area per second.

options.label: 12 m²/s
options.after: You've counted the other strip—the one due to changing width.
options.why: 12 m²/s is the width-growth contribution, not the length-growth contribution.

beats.scene: The other edge is also racing outward at 4 metres per second.
beats.question: What is the width-growth contribution?

options.label: 12 m²/s
options.after: A second strip joins the first. The banner is getting big, fast.
options.why: Width rate 4 m/s × current length 3 m = 12 m²/s.

options.label: 16 m²/s
options.after: That's the final total, but the first strip hasn't been added yet.
options.why: The width strip is 4 × 3 = 12. The total becomes 16 only after adding the other strip.

options.label: 4 m²/s
options.after: You've counted the narrow strip twice.
options.why: 4 m²/s came from length growth. Width growth uses the 3-metre current length.

beats.scene: The printer is hovering over the 'rush order' button.
beats.question: What's the banner's total area-growth rate right now?

options.label: 16 m²/s
options.after: The printer gets an honest number. The banner does not overflow the stage.
options.why: The two strip contributions add: 1 × 4 + 4 × 3 = 4 + 12 = 16 m²/s.

options.label: 4 m²/s, because 1 × 4.
options.after: The printer gets the product of two rates, not an area rate.
options.why: Two rates multiply to m²/s². You need each rate paired with the other edge's current length.

options.label: 48 m²/s, because 3 × 4 × 4.
options.after: The banner budget explodes for no physical reason.
options.why: This triple product counts dimensions incorrectly. Differentiate length × width by adding the two strip contributions.

subject: physics
title: The world's smallest ski stunt
setup: A 2 kg sled drops 5 metres. You need to predict the speed before anyone tries the stunt. Use g = 10 m/s² to keep the arithmetic friendly.
win: The sled finishes safely, and your energy budget balances. You even accounted for the energy that became heat.
detour: You found out why a squared speed isn't a speed. The stunt crew makes another calculation before the next run.

beats.scene: At the top, the 2 kg sled has gravitational energy available from the 5 m drop.
beats.question: How much energy is available?

options.label: 100 joules
options.after: The clipboard reads 100 J. That's your entire starting budget.
options.why: mgh = 2 × 10 × 5 = 100 J. This is the energy that can become kinetic or be transferred elsewhere.

options.label: 10 joules
options.after: The stunt coordinator asks where the height went.
options.why: 10 is g in m/s²; the complete energy needs mass and height as well.

options.label: 50 joules
options.after: Half the budget has mysteriously disappeared.
options.why: g × h is 50, but multiplying by the 2 kg mass gives 100 J.

beats.scene: In a frictionless run, all 100 J becomes kinetic energy. The formula is ½mv².
beats.question: What's the sled's final speed?

options.label: 10 m/s
options.after: The stunt lands exactly on the predicted mark.
options.why: 100 = ½ × 2 × v², so v² = 100. Speed is the square root: 10 m/s.

options.label: 100 m/s
options.after: That's a spectacularly unsafe forecast.
options.why: 100 is v², which has units m²/s². The speed is its square root, 10 m/s.

options.label: 50 m/s
options.after: The sled doesn't come close to your forecast.
options.why: Dividing 100 by mass isn't the end. You still need to solve for v² and take a square root.

beats.scene: The snow is rougher on the next run. Exactly 36 J transfers to heat.
beats.question: How fast does the sled finish this time?

options.label: 8 m/s
options.after: The slower arrival matches your new plan. The crew cheers the spreadsheet.
options.why: 100 − 36 = 64 J kinetic. With 2 kg, 64 = ½ × 2 × v², so v = 8 m/s.

options.label: 64 m/s
options.after: You read squared speed as ordinary speed again.
options.why: 64 is v². The square root gives 8 m/s.

options.label: 10 m/s; heat doesn't affect speed.
options.after: The rough snow slows the sled. The finish marker is in the wrong place.
options.why: The 36 J thermal transfer leaves only 64 J for movement. Conservation of total energy still holds.

subject: medicine
title: The detective and the suspicious test
setup: A fictional screening program runs 10,000 tests. The test is 99% sensitive and 95% specific. You're the one who has to explain a positive result without frightening anyone.
win: You avoid the classic screening trap: a very sensitive test isn't the same as a 99% chance that any positive patient has the condition.
detour: The case shows why a test result needs its base rate. The next question is about real groups of people, not a percentage taken out of context.

beats.scene: The condition affects 1% of this illustrative population.
beats.question: Of 10,000 people, how many actually have it?

options.after: The affected group has 100 people. The other 9,900 matter too.
options.why: One percent of 10,000 is 100. The test's false positives will come from the 9,900 unaffected people.

options.after: You've inverted the prevalence. Nearly everyone would have the condition.
options.why: 9,900 is the 99% who do not have the condition.

options.after: The detective asks you to calculate one percent, not nearly ten.
options.why: One percent is 0.01 × 10,000 = 100.

beats.scene: Among the 100 affected people, sensitivity catches 99. Among 9,900 unaffected people, specificity is 95%.
beats.question: How many unaffected people test positive anyway?

options.after: The false-positive pile is almost five times the true-positive pile.
options.why: False-positive rate = 5%. Five percent of 9,900 = 495.

options.after: That would be 5% of only 100 people, the wrong group.
options.why: Specificity refers to people without the condition, so start with 9,900.

options.after: Those are the true positives in the affected group, not the false positives.
options.why: Sensitivity catches 99 affected people. False positives come from the unaffected group.

beats.scene: You have 99 true positives and 495 false positives. The report needs a plain-language interpretation.
beats.question: Approximately what share of positive tests actually comes from affected people?

options.label: About 17%
options.after: You explain the result without equating a positive screen with a diagnosis.
options.why: 99/(99+495) = 99/594 ≈ 16.7%. This is an educational calculation, not personal medical advice.

options.after: The detective points to 495 other people holding positive results.
options.why: 99% is sensitivity among affected people. The share of positive results that are true is a different probability.

options.after: You've quoted the test's specificity, which answers another question.
options.why: Specificity measures negative results among unaffected people, not the likelihood of having the condition given a positive result.

subject: business
title: The pop-up shop's shipping surprise
kicker: Run the shop for ninety seconds
setup: Your new snack box sells for $40. Ingredients and packaging cost $14; fulfillment labor costs $5; shipping starts at $7. A viral video just made orders jump.
win: The shop survives the viral moment. You know what each order really contributes before fixed expenses.
detour: The shop stays open, but the margin lesson sticks: shipping changes can wipe out a surprisingly large part of contribution.

beats.scene: A new order appears. Rent, software and monthly overhead are still waiting in the background.
beats.question: How much contribution does one $40 box generate before fixed expenses?

options.after: Fourteen dollars hits the contribution bucket—not the profit account.
options.why: Variable cost is 14 + 5 + 7 = $26. Price 40 − variable cost 26 = $14 contribution.

options.after: You've picked the amount spent, not the amount left.
options.why: $26 is total variable cost per box; only $14 remains to cover fixed costs.

options.after: Revenue looks great until the shipping invoices arrive.
options.why: A $40 sale is not $40 of contribution. Every additional box incurs variable costs.

beats.scene: Your marketing partner says: 'Amazing! We're making $14 profit on every box.'
beats.question: What do you tell them?

options.label: That's contribution. We still owe fixed expenses.
options.after: They cross out 'profit' and write 'before overhead.' The spreadsheet survives.
options.why: Contribution covers fixed expenses first. Profit comes after those fixed costs are also paid.

options.label: Exactly. We can spend the full $14.
options.after: The rent payment sends a polite but forceful reminder.
options.why: Spending all contribution leaves nothing for fixed expenses.

options.label: No. Every box loses $26.
options.after: The team panics unnecessarily.
options.why: $26 is variable cost; each $40 sale still contributes a positive $14 before fixed expenses.

beats.scene: Shipping jumps from $7 to $11 just as orders go viral.
beats.question: What's the new contribution per box?

options.after: You adjust the forecast before the celebration gets expensive.
options.why: New variable cost = 14 + 5 + 11 = $30, so contribution is $40 − $30 = $10.

options.label: $14; the selling price didn't move.
options.after: The carrier invoice disagrees.
options.why: Variable costs changed even though price stayed $40. Contribution falls dollar for dollar.

options.label: $3; subtract the new shipping bill twice.
options.after: The spreadsheet makes the viral hit look much worse than it is.
options.why: The old $7 was already included in the original variable cost. Add only the $4 increase to the cost baseline.
